title: How To Handle An Argumentative Student
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin outlines how to handle students who try to draw a teacher into an argument, whether by challenging a decision, questioning fairness, or invoking a previous teacher's methods. He identifies students' motives as testing the teacher, derailing the lesson, or attempting to wrest control of the classroom, and warns that engaging in back-and-forth debate effectively grants every student license to do the same. The article offers three response modes depending on how the challenge is raised: enforcing a consequence without comment when a student calls out without raising a hand, briefly acknowledging but not debating when a hand is raised properly, and genuinely listening on the rare occasion a student may have a valid point worth considering. Central to all three is a brief pause before responding and a swift return to normal instruction afterward, showing no visible frustration or annoyance. The piece frames consistent avoidance of arguments as essential to maintaining leadership and preventing challenges from spreading throughout the class.
points: Students provoke arguments to test the teacher, derail the lesson, or attempt to wrest control of the classroom.
Engaging in back-and-forth debate with one student effectively grants every other student implicit license to challenge the teacher too.

—Which effectively gives license to every student in your class to do the same. Before you know it, you’re being challenged on all sides.

In this case, it’s best not to address their comment at all. Simply enforce a consequence and move on. This is a powerful move that will almost always squash their challenge altogether—which is your goal.
If the student does raise their hand, you can just say, “Hmm, I’ll think about it. Thanks for your input.” Then immediately do it your way or continue on without another word.
A pause helps. Don’t answer at first. Bite your tongue and wait a few awkward seconds. Let their argument starter hang in the air like a bad curve ball.
Handling it this way will effectively remove all arguments and challenges from your classroom. No more battles or disagreements or feeling as if you’re losing control of your class.
